question: At a math contest, \(57\) students are wearing blue shirts, and another \(75\) students are wearing yellow shirts. The \(132\) students are assigned into \(66\) pairs. In exactly \(23\) of these pairs, both students are wearing blue shirts. In how many pairs are both students wearing yellow shirts?
solution:
Any blue-shirted student outside the all-blue pairs must have a yellow-shirted partner, so counting the remaining blue students determines the mixed pairs.

The \(23\) all-blue pairs contain \(2\cdot23=46\) blue-shirted students. This leaves \(57-46=11\) blue-shirted students, each in a different mixed pair. These mixed pairs therefore use exactly \(11\) yellow-shirted students.

The remaining \(75-11=64\) yellow-shirted students all belong to all-yellow pairs. Each pair contains two students, so the number of all-yellow pairs is
\[
\frac{64}{2}=\boxed{32},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Mixed pairs contain equal numbers of the two colors, so they contribute nothing to the difference between the yellow and blue totals.

There are \(75-57=18\) more yellow-shirted students than blue-shirted students. Each all-yellow pair contributes \(2\) to this difference, while each all-blue pair contributes \(-2\). Thus there must be \(18/2=9\) more all-yellow pairs than all-blue pairs.

Since there are \(23\) all-blue pairs, the number of all-yellow pairs is
\[
23+9=\boxed{32},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

reference.question: At a math contest, \(57\) students are wearing blue shirts, and another \(75\) students are wearing yellow shirts. The \(132\) students are assigned into \(66\) pairs. In exactly \(23\) of these pairs, both students are wearing blue shirts. In how many pairs are both students wearing yellow shirts?
reference.solution:
Method 1: Find the mixed pairs first

Any blue-shirted student outside the all-blue pairs must have a yellow-shirted partner, so counting the remaining blue students determines the mixed pairs.

The \(23\) all-blue pairs contain \(2\cdot23=46\) blue-shirted students. This leaves \(57-46=11\) blue-shirted students, each in a different mixed pair. These mixed pairs therefore use exactly \(11\) yellow-shirted students.

The remaining \(75-11=64\) yellow-shirted students all belong to all-yellow pairs. Each pair contains two students, so the number of all-yellow pairs is
\[
\frac{64}{2}=\boxed{32},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

Method 2: Compare the color totals

Mixed pairs contain equal numbers of the two colors, so they contribute nothing to the difference between the yellow and blue totals.

There are \(75-57=18\) more yellow-shirted students than blue-shirted students. Each all-yellow pair contributes \(2\) to this difference, while each all-blue pair contributes \(-2\). Thus there must be \(18/2=9\) more all-yellow pairs than all-blue pairs.

Since there are \(23\) all-blue pairs, the number of all-yellow pairs is
\[
23+9=\boxed{32},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

nodes.description: Understand the concept of a unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b with b ≠ 0, and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship. For example, “This recipe has a ratio of 3 cups of flour to 4 cups of sugar, so there is 3/4 cup of flour for each cup of sugar.” “We paid \$75 for 15 hamburgers, which is a rate of \$5 per hamburger."* *Expectations for unit rates in this grade are limited to non-complex fractions.
nodes.label: 6.RP.A.2

nodes.description: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions , including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities measured in like or different units. For example, if a person walks 1/2 mile in each 1/4 hour, compute the unit rate as the complex fraction 1/2/1/4 miles per hour, equivalently 2 miles per hour.
nodes.label: 7.RP.A.1

nodes.description: Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed. For example, if it took 7 hours to mow 4 lawns, then at that rate, how many lawns could be mowed in 35 hours? At what rate were lawns being mowed?
nodes.label: 6.RP.A.3b

nodes.description: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities. For example, “The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every 2 wings there was 1 beak.” “For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes.”
nodes.label: 6.RP.A.1
